title: Foundations
summary: Arrays, hash maps, two pointers and stacks: the everyday moves every harder technique is built from.

modules.title: Arrays & Hashing
modules.summary: What array operations cost, and how hash maps trade memory for one-pass solutions.

lessons.title: Arrays and what operations cost
lessons.body_md:
An array stores its elements side by side in memory. That one fact explains most of what arrays are good and bad at: the address of element `i` is `start + i × size`, so reading `a[i]` takes the same time whether the array holds ten elements or ten million.

## Four costs to keep in your head

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Read or write `a[i]` | O(1) | one address calculation |
| Scan every element | O(n) | each element is touched once |
| Insert or delete at the front | O(n) | everything after it shifts by one |
| Append at the end (dynamic array) | O(1) amortized | an occasional resize copies, averaged out |

Most array problems are about turning a solution that re-scans the array many times into one that scans it once.

## Counting the work in a brute force

The most direct way to find a duplicate is to compare every pair. Run it and watch the number of comparisons as the input doubles:

```python run
def has_duplicate(nums):
    comparisons = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            comparisons += 1
            if nums[i] == nums[j]:
                return True, comparisons
    return False, comparisons

for n in [10, 20, 40, 80]:
    found, work = has_duplicate(list(range(n)))  # no duplicates: the worst case
    print(f"n = {n:3}  comparisons = {work}")
```

Doubling `n` roughly quadruples the work. With nothing repeated, the pair loop makes exactly this many comparisons, which grows like n²:

$$
\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}
$$

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n²)" space="O(1)"}
The pair-by-pair check needs no extra memory, but its running time is quadratic: 100,000 elements means about five billion comparisons.
:::

## Sort first, then scan once

If equal values sat next to each other, one pass would be enough to spot them. Sorting puts them there:

```python run
def has_duplicate_sorted(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)            # O(n log n), returns a new list
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):  # O(n)
        if nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            return True
    return False

print(has_duplicate_sorted([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))  # True
print(has_duplicate_sorted([2, 7, 1, 8]))     # False
```

That brings the cost down to O(n log n). The next lesson gets it to O(n) by remembering what has already been seen.

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="sorted() versus .sort()"}
`sorted(nums)` returns a new list; `nums.sort()` reorders the caller's list in place. Quietly mutating an input you were handed is a classic source of bugs in larger programs.
:::

:::question{slug=contains-duplicate}

lessons.title: Hash maps: remember what you have seen
Counting and precomputing
lessons.body_md:
Plenty of problems reduce to "how many of each?". A frequency map — value → count — answers that in one pass, and two frequency maps can be compared in O(n).

## Counting

```python run
from collections import Counter

word = "mississippi"
counts = Counter(word)
print(counts.most_common(2))  # the two most frequent letters

# The same thing without the library:
manual = {}
for ch in word:
    manual[ch] = manual.get(ch, 0) + 1
print(manual)
```

## Anagrams have equal counts

Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character appears the same number of times in both. Count one string up and the other down; they are anagrams if every count ends at zero:

```python run
def is_anagram(s, t):
    if len(s) != len(t):
        return False
    counts = {}
    for a, b in zip(s, t):
        counts[a] = counts.get(a, 0) + 1
        counts[b] = counts.get(b, 0) - 1
    return all(v == 0 for v in counts.values())

print(is_anagram("listen", "silent"))  # True
print(is_anagram("rat", "car"))        # False
```

:::callout{kind=note}
Sorting both strings and comparing them also works, in O(n log n). Counting is O(n), and with a fixed alphabet (say 26 lowercase letters) the map never grows past 26 entries, so its extra space is O(1).
:::

## Precomputing from both sides

Counting is one kind of precomputation; prefix and suffix products are another. To get, for every index, the product of all the *other* elements without dividing, combine what lies to its left with what lies to its right:

$$
\text{answer}_i = \left(\prod_{j < i} a_j\right) \cdot \left(\prod_{j > i} a_j\right)
$$

```python run
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):              # out[i] = product of everything left of i
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):  # multiply in everything right of i
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

print(product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # [24, 12, 8, 6]
print(product_except_self([2, 0, 5]))     # [0, 10, 0]
```

:::callout{kind=pitfall title="Why not divide?"}
Dividing the total product by `a[i]` breaks as soon as the array contains a zero. Two passes of prefix and suffix products never divide.
:::

:::question{slug=valid-anagram}

:::question{slug=product-of-array-except-self}

checkpoint.prompt_md: On average, how long does `x in seen` take when `seen` is a Python `set`?
checkpoint.explanation_md: A set hashes `x` and jumps straight to its bucket. Only heavy collisions — rare with a good hash function — make a lookup slower.

checkpoint.prompt_md: In one-pass Two Sum, why do you look up `target - x` **before** storing `x`?
choices: So an element never pairs with itself
checkpoint.explanation_md: With target 6 and a single 3, storing first would let the 3 find itself. Looking up first only ever pairs `x` with earlier elements.

checkpoint.prompt_md: How many comparisons does the brute-force pair check make on 100 distinct elements?
Which class from Python's `collections` module builds a frequency map (value → count) in one call?
checkpoint.explanation_md: `Counter(iterable)` counts every element in one pass; `most_common(k)` then lists the k most frequent.

lessons.title: Pointers from both ends
Read and write pointers

checkpoint.prompt_md: Pair sum on a sorted array: `a[l] + a[r]` is larger than the target. What is safe to do?
checkpoint.explanation_md: `a[r]` is too big even with the smallest partner left (`a[l]`), so no remaining pair can use it. Dropping it is safe.

checkpoint.prompt_md: How much extra memory does the sorted two-pointer pair search use?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Just two indices and a sum — constant space. The hash-map version needs O(n).

checkpoint.prompt_md: In the read/write filter, what does everything before the `write` index hold?
choices: The kept elements, in their original order
checkpoint.explanation_md: `write` only advances after copying a kept element, so `a[0..write)` is always the finished, in-order answer.

checkpoint.prompt_md: Three sum sorts the input, then runs a pair search for each fixed element. What is its overall time complexity, in Big-O?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Sorting is O(n log n); then n fixed elements each run a linear pair search, O(n²) in total, which dominates.

lessons.title: Last in, first out
The monotonic stack
lessons.body_md:
Some questions ask, for every element, about the *nearest* element to one side that is bigger or smaller: the next warmer day, the next taller building, how far a bar can stretch in a histogram. Checking every later element costs O(n²). A **monotonic stack** answers all of them in one pass.

## Next greater element

Keep a stack of indices whose answer is still unknown. Their values decrease from bottom to top — each is waiting for something bigger. When a new value arrives it is the answer for every waiting index with a smaller value, so pop those and record it:

```python run
def next_greater(nums):
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []                        # waiting indices; their values decrease
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            answer[stack.pop()] = x   # x is the first bigger value to the right
        stack.append(i)
    return answer

print(next_greater([2, 1, 5, 3, 4, 6, 1]))  # [5, 5, 6, 4, 6, -1, -1]
```

## Why it is linear

The inner `while` can pop many items at once, which looks quadratic. But each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so over the whole run:

$$
\text{pushes} + \text{pops} \le 2n
$$

:::callout{kind=complexity time="O(n)" space="O(n)"}
Amortized O(1) per element: the occasional expensive step (many pops) is paid for by the cheap pushes that came before it.
:::

## Largest rectangle in a histogram

The same idea finds, for each bar, the widest rectangle of its height. That rectangle stops at the nearest *shorter* bar on each side. Keep the stack increasing; when a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar popped has just found its right boundary, and the bar beneath it on the stack is its left boundary:

```python run
def largest_rectangle(heights):
    bars = heights + [0]            # a final 0 pops whatever is left
    stack = []                      # indices, heights increasing
    best = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(bars):
        while stack and bars[stack[-1]] > h:
            top = stack.pop()
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1   # nearest shorter bar on the left
            best = max(best, bars[top] * (i - left - 1))
        stack.append(i)
    return best

print(largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))  # 10: height 5, width 2
```

:::callout{kind=note title="Rule of thumb"}
"Nearest bigger or smaller element to the left or right" means a monotonic stack. Keep it decreasing to find the next *greater* element, increasing to find the next *smaller*.
:::

:::question{slug=largest-rectangle-in-histogram}

checkpoint.prompt_md: Which string does the bracket checker reject *only* because of its final `not stack` check?
checkpoint.explanation_md: `((` never meets a wrong closer; it fails because two openers are still on the stack when the input ends.

checkpoint.prompt_md: Using a Python list as a stack, which pair of operations are both O(1)?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Working at the end of a dynamic array is O(1) (amortized for `append`). Anything at the front shifts every element.

checkpoint.prompt_md: In the next-greater-element pass, the values of the indices on the stack, read from bottom to top, are…
checkpoint.explanation_md: Anything smaller than the incoming value is popped before it is pushed, so what stays below is at least as big: the stack decreases toward the top.

checkpoint.prompt_md: What is the total running time of the monotonic-stack pass over n elements?
checkpoint.explanation_md: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once — at most 2n stack operations in total.

checkpoint.prompt_md: Which data structure remembers the most recent unmatched opening bracket?
checkpoint.explanation_md: The newest unmatched opener is exactly the top of a stack, which is what the next closer must match.
